summary: The formula entity page covers CanonicalFormula, a saved macro expression, bounded only by a hostile-input ceiling, such as a word count over the chat plus a roll, made once and run anywhere. A formula is macro text and nothing else, so what it can do is what the macro engine gives it, including Bunzai's own mentions, lastmention, tally and odds macros, and its decoder checks only shape and size. The page explains that a tool runs a formula through its formula action on the macro context the turn built its prompt from, handed to the tools once the prompt is built, and that the run happens on a copy, with any variable write refused out loud and blank or failing formulas refused too. The Editing section describes the formula editor and its Try rail, which runs the text on a copy of a scene through the formula-try route.

sections.title: Where formulas run
sections.summary: A tool runs a formula through its formula action, described on the tool page, and the model is told what the formula renders. The formula reads the macro context the turn built its prompt from: the card, the persona, the history before the message being answered, and the variables as the prompt left them. That context is handed to the tools through ToolsContext.macros once the prompt is built, because tools are made before the prompt exists but called after it, and a call that somehow arrives before the context is there is refused instead of running against an empty context. Tools are the only place formulas run today.

sections.title: Safety
sections.summary: runFormulaReadOnly runs the formula on a structuredClone of the macro context, so nothing it touches reaches the scene. A run that would change a variable, through setvar, state.set, once, ask_in_reply, pick and the like, is refused in words naming the macros, and a message holding a write macro makes formulas that read message text fail. Blank formulas and macro errors are refused. A formula has no step number of its own: the tool loop owns a time budget for all of a reply's tool calls, a setting with a default (shown in seconds in Settings), hands each run what is left as a deadline, and the macro engine checks that clock between nodes, after every handler and inside the word macros' loops, so a run that passes it answers with the error, never as finished. A formula shares the chat's messages, so the positional word index is built once and a phrase costs what its rarest word costs. Each call takes its own seed.

sections.title: Editing
sections.summary: A formula opens in the Workbench's formula editor: what it is for, the formula text in the app's code editor with macro chips under it, covering the chat-watching macros, odds and tracker plus an All macros reference, and a Try it rail. Try runs the text as it stands, saved or not, on a copy of the scene you pick through the formula-try route, which reads the scene as it stands with the assembler a send runs, then runs the text through the read-only formula path inside the tool time budget. It answers the result, or the words for why it stopped, such as a variable it would change, a macro error or the spent budget, with how long it took. It needs no connection and builds the whole scene with no window to fit, so entries a send would trim can still feed the macros. Nothing in the scene changes and no model is asked. A save with nothing edited sends nothing. New formula saves a blank one, refused when run until it has text.
